name: Reactions to the Kennedy Assassination News
description: The car is packed with the Husband, Wife, Jim, Children, Dog, and Mother-in-Law. Jim sits in the back, wearing torn black chinos and a paint-spotted black t-shirt, his posture slouched. The Husband, glancing at Jim with a hint of unease, turns up the Perry Como song on the radio. Suddenly, a news flash cuts in: President John F. Kennedy has been shot in Dallas at the Texas School Book Depository. The Husband’s face twists in shock. He says something under his breath, a muffled 'What! God NO!', and quickly tries other radio stations. Jim turns to look out the window, his expression still, as if he had expected the news. The radio reports that the President has been taken to Parkland Memorial Hospital, with no word on his condition, and mentions Mrs. Kennedy. The Wife and Husband murmur in horror, 'Oh God, Oh God. Not the President for Christ's sake. Oh God—WHO'S NEXT?' Jim continues staring out the window, then says, 'Who's next!'

She begins to speak about her sister when Jim interrupts gently, saying he bets she never expected life to be this hard. He strokes her hair. She breaks down in tears and moves into his arms. A vendor openly sells LSD from a folding table. Muscle builders strain under iron, dogs dart after frisbees, and bikini-clad bodies stretch out on the sand. Jim moves slowly through the crowd, barefoot and shirtless in torn black chinos, a notebook in one hand, a paperback of Baudelaire in the other. His gaze settles on a young woman with long red hair, a yellow labrador at her side, as she weaves through the crowd.

name: The Doors Arrive in the Desert and Begin the Peyote Ritual
description: A dented red Chevrolet skids across a dry mudflat, kicking up swirling dust devils. The car comes to a stop near the edge of a cliff surrounded by deep arroyos, towering rocks, and scattered cacti. Ray, John, Robbie, and Jim step out and form a loose circle, their laughter echoing strangely under the influence of peyote. Nearby, Pam crouches at the cliff’s edge, vomiting violently as Dorothy kneels beside her, trying to comfort her. Jim climbs up a nearby dune, scanning the group. 'Everybody having a good time?' he calls out. Pam retches again. Jim watches, then touches his head as if feeling the intensity of the moment. He moves through the sand, briefly touching Pam’s face before turning sharply, pointing at the sky. 'Hawk! Hawk!' he shouts. Pam rises and begins to dance alone on the dune. Jim rejoins the others, standing among The Doors as they continue to laugh, their expressions shifting, their eyes wide, caught between euphoria and something darker.

name: Jim Describes the Serpent in the Desert
description: The red Chevrolet sits dented on the dry mudflat, dust swirling around it. John shudders. Robbie shudders. Ray shudders. Their faces tighten, eyes wide, breath shallow. The air grows still. The mood darkens.

Jim tells him that’s the point—madness is part of the divine, that Dionysus brought both ecstasy and madness, and that confusion is where creation begins. One by one, they sit in silence as Jim speaks louder, calling for them to take in all of it—fear, pain, lust—without turning away. name: Pam Reads Jim's Notebooks on the Rooftop
description: Pam sits beside Jim on a rooftop, flipping through his notebooks by the light of a lantern. The pages are filled with vivid, hallucinogenic sketches in the style of William Blake, interspersed with handwritten notes. Around them, books by Kerouac, Ginsberg, Nietzsche, Rimbaud, and others are scattered across the sleeping bag. Pam pauses, struck by the beauty of the drawings. She says she never liked poetry in school but finds the notebooks captivating. She asks what a "shaman" is, mispronouncing the word. Jim tells her a shaman is a medicine man who enters a peyote trance, draws the whole tribe into his vision, and heals them through shared experience. He adds that the same pattern appears across cultures—among the Greeks, in the story of Jesus. Some Native traditions say the first shaman invented sex, he says, and that the shaman is the one who makes people crazy. Pam looks at him and asks if he is a shaman. Jim hesitates, then says no—he only writes about it. He asks what turns her on. She replies: experience, freedom, love, now. She talks about peyote and acid, how the first time she took acid she saw God, had a friend who was both Christ and Judas, and suddenly knew that everything is one and everything is beautiful. Jim says he believes life is known through pain, through confronting death. Pam counters that life comes from recognizing beauty and seeing truth, which leads to love. She says they’re all saying the same thing: "love me and I'll love you." Jim replies that life is only known through death, that healers like Jesus sacrifice themselves. Pam asks if he loves death. He says death ends pain, that life hurts more than dying. Pam shivers and says she looks at him and sees her death, then dismisses it as ridiculous. Jim guesses her father is a schoolteacher. She’s surprised and asks how he knew. He doesn’t answer. She asks about his father. He says military. She guesses he moved around a lot. He confirms it—about eight times. She asks how many siblings he has. He says two. She says one is the pretty one. Then she tells him she loves his neck and climbs into his lap. He runs his fingers through her hair, kisses her gently. He recites a line: "...but one, the most beautiful one of all dances in a ring of fire and throws off the challenge with a shrug." Pam calls it beautiful and asks who it was written for. Jim says he wrote it for her. Her panties come off. Rousseau dangles from the moon over Venice. Jim moves with nervous excitement, awkward in the moment. Pam tells him to take his time, that there’s no hurry, that he’s all she has to do tonight. A song plays—"Well the clock says it's time to close now, I guess I'd better go now..."—as the scene fades from the rooftop. Fingers tremble like minarets. Secret alphabets pass between them. He lights another cigarette. Somewhere, the soft rhythm of "Moonlight Drive" begins to play. Ray Manzarek sits in a yoga posture, meditating quietly in the dim light.
